where: Section 1, definition of mobile host; also Quiz Q1 and Q4
problem: The definition says a mobile host changes its point of attachment 'while a session is open'. The standard definition does not require an open session: a phone that moves between cells while idle is still a mobile host, and the session is only what makes the problem hard. The chapter contradicts itself, because the Exam traps say location tracking finds an idle user, i.e. a mobile host with no session. A student will write the narrower definition and lose the point about idle hosts.
fix: Define it as: a mobile host is a computer that changes its point of attachment to the network. Then add separately: keeping an open session alive across that change is the hard part. Use the same wording in the Quiz Q1 answer, and in Q4 justify the desktop by saying its point of attachment never changes at all.

where: Section 1, 'Wireless is not the same as mobile'; repeated in Exam trap 1
problem: The laptop on a train is said to have 'no radio at all'. With no network connection of any kind it is just a laptop with no network, so it is neither mobile nor wireless in the networking sense. The intended case is a laptop that stays connected by a cable.
fix: Say: a laptop plugged into the train's wired network keeps its session while the train moves, so it is mobile but not wireless.

problem: 'In every case the payload is small and the delay matters more than the data rate' is not true of fleet tracking. A GPS position pushed every few minutes can wait; that application is delay-tolerant and needs only that the position eventually arrives.
fix: Say: for the interactive cases (payments, ticketing, telemedicine) delay matters more than the data rate; fleet tracking is delay-tolerant but needs the position to arrive reliably.

where: Section 2, Figure note and Exam trap 2
problem: Saying middleware sits between the radio link and the Internet and never inside the phone contradicts Section 2 itself, which lists safe storage of keys as a middleware job; key storage happens on the handset. Standard middleware also has a client part (a sync client, a keystore).
fix: Say: the heavy work (location lookup, authentication, sync reconciliation) is done by servers in the network, while small client pieces such as the sync client and the key store sit on the handset.

problem: The note reads 'Internet and PSTN'. The PSTN is the circuit-switched telephone network and is not on the path of a UPI request; listing it next to the Internet in a data example misleads.
fix: Change the note to 'Internet and operator core network'.

problem: Using 2²⁰ instead of 10⁶ changes the transmission time by about 5%, but it changes the total one-way time in the worked examples by well under 1%, because the 40 ms delay dominates. Saying 'the answer shifts by about 5%' overstates it.
fix: Say: this shifts the transmission time by about 5%; the total time barely moves because the delay dominates.
